prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of flat bands in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in it

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B025 first, with the same configuration I held in round 1: MacDonald and Bistritzer for the continuum-model prediction of flat bands at a magic angle, and Jarillo-Herrero for the 2018 discovery of correlated insulating and gate-tunable superconducting states. The discovery being credited is the existence of these phases at the magic angle, which is a secure experimental fact reproduced by many groups and in several moire platforms, not the pairing mechanism. The structure is prediction followed by a decisive experiment, with the twist angle as one continuous control parameter, and it can be stated in one sentence. The round-1 record shows no member contesting the phenomena themselves, only timing and attribution, and I do not think those objections outweigh the combination of originality, reproducibility and generative impact. The citation should be worded to credit the prediction and the first correlated and superconducting states, and should not claim a mechanism or imply that no flat-band signatures were seen before 2018.
statement.case_against: The strongest case against is that B025 is the youngest candidate, about eight years from the experiments, with an open pairing mechanism and uneven twist-angle disorder between samples. If a later body of results showed that the superconductivity was fragile or sample-specific, the prize would look early. The second weakness is attribution: the three-name cap leaves out Eva Andrei, whose early scanning-probe evidence of flat bands and van Hove singularities is a real experimental contribution, and I cannot settle her weight from the supplied evidence. B013 is the more mature fallback, and a reasonable member could prefer its age over my reading of B025, even though its compound credit is messier.

responses.point: Danielsson moved from B033 to B013 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, arguing it is a complete chain from theory to discovery with nearly two decades of confirmation, and that the 2016 topology prize and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang credit make the case compound.
responses.response: I accept that B013 is the more mature case and I keep it as my first alternative, and I agree with you that Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is the right trio and that the citation must stay on the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect. Where we still differ is on what maturity should mean. Your own against-statement concedes that B013 leaves the HgTe prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang outside the names, and that is a prediction-to-experiment link that the three names cannot cover, whereas in B025 the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the Jarillo-Herrero experiment are both inside the configuration. I also think the 2016 overlap you raise points slightly against B013 on novelty, so I do not see B013 as clearly ahead once attribution and overlap are counted. I was not moved to change my preference, but your argument is why B013 stays in my alternatives.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B006 with Katori and Ye as a discovery-plus-instrument prize that is not premature, resting on frequency combs (2005) and ion-clock control (2012) without duplicating them, and she notes that the redefinition of the second is undecided.
responses.response: I find your attribution argument for B006 the cleanest on the shortlist: two names, a sharp concept in magic-wavelength trapping, and independent confirmation across several national laboratories. I also take your point that familiarity should not be mistaken for consensus, and I apply the same caution to my own familiarity with condensed matter. My remaining disagreement is on novelty. You say the clock prize sits on the 2005 and 2012 base without duplicating it, but in round 1 I asked for one consistent standard on nearby recent prizes, and by that standard a third prize in frequency metrology is no freer of closeness than the 2025 prize is for B009. I would accept B006 as a fair outcome, I do not regard it as stronger than B025, and I have kept it as my second alternative.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B013 with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, arguing it is the least contested on names, and admits that Hasan's three-dimensional work is an equally decisive discovery that a three-person prize cannot also honour.
responses.response: Your honesty about the two-dimensional versus three-dimensional split is exactly the problem I see in B013: a trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp is a sound citation of the quantum spin Hall effect, but it will be read as the prize for topological insulators generally, and then the omission of Hasan and of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang looks like a real hole. You argue the 2016 overlap is limited, and I agree that the 2016 prize did not cover this line directly. I still think the attribution problem in B025, namely Andrei, is smaller in kind, because her work is early supporting evidence for the physics that the prediction and the discovery already name. I do not move, but I agree that the quality of B013 is not in doubt and that a vote for it would be defensible.

responses.point: Kroll says that for the optical lattice clock the evidence is the least dependent on interpretation, that it is confirmed by independent laboratories agreeing with each other, and that the record in frequency metrology is already dense.
responses.response: The point about interpretation is a fair one and it tells in favour of B006 when I weigh maturity: no one doubts the 10^-18 numbers. I would turn it around only in one respect. For B025 the existence of the correlated and superconducting states is likewise independent of interpretation, because it is a transport measurement repeated by many groups, and the open question is the pairing theory. On that basis I do not think your concern about timing applies to the credited discovery. I agree with your own against-statement that the density of earlier metrology prizes is a real weight on B006, and I see no sign among the openings or round-1 statements that this concern can be dismissed.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B025 with MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, and says that if the committee judges the field too fluid, B013 or B006 are the safer, more mature choices.
responses.response: We are aligned on configuration and citation, and I want to take your safer-fallback remark seriously rather than just agree with it. I think the right test for 'too fluid' is whether the credited phenomena are still contested, and the round-1 record shows only an open mechanism question. Because you disclose adjacency to the field through two-dimensional materials and I do not, I would ask the committee to treat your support and mine as separate scientific judgements and to rest the case on reproducibility and the clarity of prediction followed by experiment. On Andrei, I still want her claim acknowledged in the discussion even though I no longer put her in the configuration.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asks in his summary whether the third name should be Bistritzer or Andrei and whether the citation can name both the prediction and the discovery without implying that flat-band signatures were unseen before 2018.
responses.response: My answer to the chair's first question is Bistritzer: the continuum model he wrote with MacDonald is the origin of the magic angle, and the 2018 experiments were explicitly motivated by it, so without it the discovery has no predicted target. To the second, I propose the citation as written above, in which the prediction is credited to a theoretical model and the discovery is limited to correlated insulating and superconducting states, which leaves Andrei's earlier scanning-probe evidence of flat bands neither contradicted nor credited. On field-neutral standards, I would apply the same rule to every candidate: weigh recent nearby prizes on novelty, not as a bar, and weigh youth by whether the credited phenomena are still disputed.

uncertainties: Whether Andrei's early scanning-probe work deserves a place in the three-name set instead of Bistritzer or MacDonald; I am relying on my memory of the historical record, not on supplied verification, and I could not resolve it from the round-1 statements either.

Whether the unresolved pairing mechanism and the twist-angle disorder justify waiting, which is the real point of disagreement with Danielsson, Kroll, Lindroth and Olsson, and whether my own reading of 'discovery of the phenomena' is too generous.
Whether the committee should treat B013 and B006 as overlapping with the 2016 prize and the 2005 and 2012 prizes to a degree that I may be applying unevenly across candidates.
Whether the superconducting-circuit prize of 2025 should weigh at all on any candidate; I do not use it for B025, B013 or B006, and I stay out of B009.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my round-1 disclosure. I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology and work in circuit and waveguide QED at Chalmers, so B009 (circuit quantum electrodynamics) is in my own subfield and I have kept it out of my configuration and alternatives and will not argue for it. Documented connections are Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson, my frequent co-author Anton Frisk Kockum and the WACQT groups, all in the superconducting-circuit area. No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B025, B013 or B006. Olsson is a Chalmers colleague, and that does not bear on any of these three ballots.
